source.title: Understanding quantum machine learning also requires rethinking generalization
source.authors: Elies Gil-Fuster; J. Eisert; Carlos Bravo-Prieto

record.tranche_reason: The study runs randomization experiments on a quantum neural network, comparing training and test errors for natural and corrupted quantum data. This is a conceptual analogue of the claim, but it does not test the specified classical models or settings.
record.gate_note: The paper tests a quantum convolutional neural network on quantum phase recognition. Its QCNN results do not match the classical datasets and model conditions named in V1–V8, so the rows are recorded under versions ["none"]. The paper also gives theoretical constructions for fitting arbitrary labels; those are not experimental outcomes and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study experimentally reproduces the memorization–generalization comparison in quantum circuits, but V1 concerns classical neural networks. Quantum circuits on quantum-state inputs are a different kind of system, as the authors explicitly emphasize. No results test V2–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is substantially accurate. More precisely, the authors argue that distribution-independent bounds uniform over the hypothesis family must be uninformative in the tested small-sample regimes where random data can be fit. They do not claim existing theorems are false or explain successful generalization. Their analytical memorization constructions require conditioning or distinguishability assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the randomization-test approach associated with the original classical study, but applies it to a quantum convolutional neural network, quantum phase recognition, and quantum-state data.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-set size and label-corruption fraction change the observed gap or test error. For random states, the gap height differs slightly with class frequencies.

fits_no_version.finding: With small training sets, the same QCNN architecture and optimization procedure fit uniformly random labels with a gap near 0.75, while successful generalization is reported on original phase labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantum circuits can combine random-label memorization capacity with generalization on structured quantum data.

fits_no_version.finding: For 8-qubit QCNNs with N = 4, 6, or 8, training accuracy remains 100% while test error increases with corruption and approaches 75%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantum circuits can fit corrupted labels while their held-out performance deteriorates as data-label correlations disappear.

fits_no_version.finding: QCNNs perfectly fit small sets of randomized quantum inputs without exceeding the applicable guessing baseline on test data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QCNNs can memorize randomized quantum inputs despite their architectural emphasis on local correlations.

record.problems: The numerical experiments use one architecture and one quantum phase-recognition task, with small training sets. Many curve values are presented only in figures; the text gives no exact uncertainty values. The authors state that these experiments do not study the generalization capacity of state-of-the-art QML generally.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported experimental condition or measure bearing on the claim was identified for extraction. The theoretical finite-sample expressivity constructions are not empirical result rows.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label generalization in classical neural networks using the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as classical ReLU networks widen beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of generalization gaps; sharpness is only suggested for future work.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: T6 applies relative to the supplied versions, despite substantive original experiments on a quantum analogue of V1. The cannot_determine states concern applicability to those versions, not uncertainty that the reported quantum effects occurred.

versions.untested_parts: The specified classical architectures, datasets, and training recipes.
Width sweeps of one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected classical networks on image datasets.
Comparisons of adaptive optimizers and SGD on image and language benchmarks.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions in the specified fully connected and convolutional classifiers.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and MNIST.

rows.value: Random-label gap close to 0.75; training accuracy perfect for the reported high-gap regime, with test accuracy at random-guessing level.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation across different experiment repetitions; exact values not stated.
rows.locator: Results, section C(c); Fig. 3(a) and its caption
rows.note: Text identifies the largest random-label gap for training sets up to size N = 10. It describes the curves by qubit count but does not give separate numeric values for each count.
rows.check: The quantum result does not establish any listed version. The near-0.75 gap and perfect random-label fit apply to the small-training-set regime, particularly N ≤ 10; fitting deteriorates at larger N. Figure 3(a) aggregates across qubit counts rather than reporting separate curves for each count. Locator should be section II.C(a), not II.C(c).

rows.subject: QCNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on data with varying fractions of randomly corrupted labels; test error measured after convergence.

conditions.value: quantum phase recognition; partially corrupted labels

rows.measure: Test error after convergence; training accuracy.
rows.baseline: No corruption, r = 0; exact test error not stated.
rows.value: Training accuracy reached 100% in all repetitions. Test error steadily increased with corruption and converged to 75% as r approached 1.
rows.locator: Results, section C(b); Fig. 3(b) and its caption
rows.note: The text describes the test-error trend and endpoint, but does not report per-corruption numerical values.
rows.check: The reported 100% training accuracy and test-error increase to 75% are supported, but concern quantum circuits rather than the systems named in V1. Test sets are drawn from the corresponding corrupted distribution Dr, so intermediate-corruption test error is not evaluation exclusively against clean labels.

rows.measure: Empirical generalization gap and test accuracy.
rows.baseline: Real data and random-label data comparisons; exact values not stated.
rows.value: The QCNN could perfectly fit the training set for few data; test accuracy failed to surpass random guessing. Gap curve described as similar in shape to random labels.

rows.check: This measures memorization of randomized quantum inputs, outside all listed versions. Perfect fitting is restricted to few training examples. The random-state guessing baseline reflects unequal class frequencies and should not automatically be assigned the uniform-label 75% error baseline.

relation.reason: The paper discusses the classical memorization–generalization finding and adapts its randomization experiments to quantum models without testing a listed version.

tranche.reason: The results concern quantum circuits on quantum-state inputs, outside the classical systems specified by V1–V8. The rules require the same kind of system for a version link.

source_check.notes: Perfect random-label fitting and the near-0.75 gap concern small training sets, especially N ≤ 10. Test sets independently follow each experiment's corresponding distribution; the random-state guessing baseline reflects unequal class frequencies.
